claims.claim: The test would have found about a one-tenth change in the average preference significant.
claims.source: Importantly, our test would have found about a one-tenth change in the average preference significant.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the statistical power of the test.

claims.claim: When sessions with IPs close to 1:1 were excluded, the ANOVA still found no significant effects on indifference points.
claims.source: To test this possibility, we removed sessions within a conservative 1.45:1 preference based on an empirical distribution of variance (see Materials and Methods, 19 session pairs were excluded) and reran the two-way ANOVA. Despite our focus on sessions with strong preferences (mean IP for all conditions: 2.07), this analysis still found neither significant main effects (Fiber: F(1,90) = 1.57, p=0.21; Laser: F(1,90) = 1.19, p=0.28) nor any interaction (F(1,90) = 0.87, p=0.35).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the three-way interaction or any two-way interactions on indifference points.
claims.source: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the critical three-way interaction of Laser*Fiber*Time (F(2,141) = 0.08, p=0.92), nor any of the two-way interactions (Laser*Time: F(2,141) = 1.58, p=0.21; Fiber*Time F(2,141) = 0.35, p=0.70; Laser*Fiber (F1,141)=0.73, p=0.40).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: There was a main effect of Time on indifference points, likely due to variations in preferences across the three pellets used for each time block.
claims.source: There was a main effect of Time (F(1,141) = 5.97, p=5.0e-3), which is likely due to the variations in the preferences across the three pellets used for each of the three time blocks.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and the authors' interpretation.

claims.claim: When analyzing only the first 29.9% of each session, the two-way ANOVA found no significant effect of inactivation on indifference points.
claims.source: To determine whether an effect of inactivation was apparent at the beginning of a behavioral session, we included the minimum number of trials for each offer for which we could determine a reasonable estimate of the IP (n = 4 for each of the 11 offers, for both laser-on and –off trial-types, 88 trials total) which was on average, the first 29.9% of the session. We then reran the two-way ANOVA test on this early session behavior. Neither the critical interaction effect of Laser*Fiber nor the main effects displayed a significant effect of inactivation (see Supplementary file 2 for ANOVA results).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 2 containing the statistical results.

claims.claim: A repeated measures two-way ANOVA on inverse slope measures revealed no significant main effects or interaction.
claims.source: A repeated measures two-way ANOVA on these measures revealed no significant main effect of either Laser (F(1,147) = 0.69, p=0.41) or Fiber (F(1,147) = 0.11, p=0.74) nor any significant effect of the critical interaction term Laser*Fiber (F(1,147) = 0.26, p=0.61).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in inverse slope when comparing the current groups to eYFP controls from a prior experiment.
claims.source: In addition, at the reviewers' request, we also compared the current groups to eYFP controls, identically trained and tested in a prior experiment, and there were no significant differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, see Supplementary file 1 for ANOVA results)(Gardner et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1, with citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Simple effects analysis showed no significant differences in inverse slope across conditions.
claims.source: Simple effects within and across factors also showed no significant differences (4 paired t-tests, n = 50, p>=0.29).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: When sessions with IPs close to 1:1 were excluded, the ANOVA still found no significant effects on inverse slope.
claims.source: We again tested whether the slope might be more affected by inactivation during sessions in which the IP is reasonably distant from equal or 1:1 preference (Figure 4D). We used the same empirical threshold, 1.45:1, that we used for testing the IPs resulting in 19 fewer session pairs entering into the analysis. We repeated the ANOVA and again found no significant effects (Laser: F(1,90) = 0.19, p=0.66; Fiber: F(1,90) = 0.74, p=0.39; Laser*Fiber: F(1,90) < 0.01 , p=0.98), and testing of the simple effects across conditions showed no effects as well (4 paired t-tests, n = 31, p>0.55).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 4D.

claims.claim: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the three-way interaction or any two-way interactions on inverse slope.
claims.source: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the critical three-way interaction of Laser*Fiber*Time (F(2,141) = 0.06, p=0.94), nor any of the two-way interactions (Laser*Time: F(2,141) = 0.04, p=0.96; Fiber*Time F(2,141) = 2.11, p=0.12; Laser*Fiber (F1,141)=0.27, p=0.61).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: There was no main effect of Time on inverse slope.
claims.source: Unlike the IP, there was no main effect of Time (F(1,141) = 0.44, p=0.64), further indicating this effect was due to variations in the preferences of the pellets used across the time blocks.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: When analyzing only the first 29.9% of each session, the critical interaction effect of Laser*Fiber on inverse slope was not significant.
claims.source: Finally, we looked at whether the slope was affected by inactivation just at the beginning of the session. As explained for the IP analysis, we narrowed our data to the first 4 trials of each offer (on average the first 29.9% of each session) and reran the two-way ANOVA test on this early session behavior. The critical interaction effect of Laser*Fiber was not significant.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 2 containing the statistical results.

claims.claim: The main effect of Laser on inverse slope was significant in the early session analysis.
claims.source: The main effect of Laser was significant. Further analysis revealed a significant difference in the simple effects between the laser-on and –off trials in the blocked fiber condition, but not in the patent fiber condition (see Supplementary file 2 for ANOVA results).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 2 containing the statistical results.

claims.claim: Rats show transitive behavior on the economic choice task when choosing between multiple pellet-types across days.
claims.source: Rats show transitive behavior on our task when choosing between multiple pellet-types across days.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about observed behavior.

claims.claim: Transitive behavior implies that rats have a consistent and relatively stable value space onto which they map different goods.
claims.source: This implies that rats have a consistent and relatively stable value space onto which they map different goods in our task.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed transitive behavior.

claims.claim: The rats' behavior was generally transitive, with only small, seemingly random fluctuations between laser-on and laser-off trials.
claims.source: A comparison of these points for laser-on versus laser-off trials in blocked versus patent sessions demonstrates that the rats' behavior was again generally transitive, with only small, seemingly random fluctuations between the laser-on and laser-off trial types.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed transitivity data.

claims.claim: The small fluctuations in transitivity were unaffected by whether or not the fiber was patent to allow inactivation.
claims.source: Critically the points and these small fluctuations were unaffected by whether or not the fiber was patent to allow inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed transitivity data.

claims.claim: A repeated-measures, two-way ANOVA on transitivity values found no main effects or interaction.
claims.source: To confirm this, we performed a repeated-measures, two-way ANOVA comparing the single transitivity values; this analysis found neither main effects nor any interaction (Laser: F(1,42) = 0.54, p=0.47; Fiber: F(1,42) = 3.21, p=0.08; Laser*Fiber: F(1,42) = 0.54, p=0.47).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: A repeated measures ANOVA on the distances between paired transitivity points found no effect of fiber type.
claims.source: To determine whether these distances were affected by inactivation, we ran a repeated measures ANOVA with the fiber-type as the single factor on the distances of the pairs of laser-on and –off trials and found no effect of Fiber: F(1,14) = 0.13, p=0.73.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: Resting membrane potential was significantly hyperpolarized by 10 s light exposure in medial OFC neurons expressing NpHR-YFP.
claims.source: We then performed whole cell current clamp recordings in neurons (n = 10) transfected with NpHR-YFP and assessed the effect of 593 nm light exposure (Figure 6A). Resting membrane potential was significantly hyperpolarized by 10 s light exposure (One-way ANOVA, F(1.06,9.49) = 26.42, p= 5.0e-4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiology data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The hyperpolarization effect was maximal at the onset but maintained significant hyperpolarization in the steady state condition.
claims.source: The effect was maximal at the onset (peak) but maintained significant hyperpolarization in the steady state condition.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: Repetitive firing activity elicited by current injection was significantly inhibited by concurrent light exposure.
claims.source: In addition, repetitive firing activity elicited by a square pulse current injection of 400 pA was significantly inhibited by concurrent light exposure (Paired t-test, t(5) = 4.05, p=0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiology data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Following light exposure, direct current injection elicited fewer spikes per unit of current as evidenced by a rightward shift in the input-output curve.
claims.source: Following light exposure, direct current injection elicited fewer spikes per unit of current as evidenced by a rightward shift in the input-output curve (Figure 6B)(Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(11, 55)=4.3, p=1.0e-4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiology data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 6B.

claims.claim: A repeated measures ANOVA on the progressive ratio breaking point revealed a significant main effect of Fiber.
claims.source: A repeated measures ANOVA (rat and run were used as blocking factors) performed on the breaking point, corresponding to the number of pellets achieved, revealed a significant main effect of Fiber (F(1,10) = 9.97, p=0.01).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: The effect of fiber type on progressive ratio breaking point was robust with 7 of 8 blocked/patent pairs trending in the same direction.
claims.source: This effect was robust with 7 of the eight blocked/patent pairs trending in the same direction (Figure 7A left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7A showing the individual data points.

claims.claim: An ANOVA on total lever presses in the progressive ratio task revealed a significant main effect of Fiber.
claims.source: An ANOVA with the same design yet performed on the total lever presses also revealed a significant main effect of Fiber (F(1,10) = 7.85, p=0.02) (Figure 7B right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Prolonged inhibition did not result in decreased motor activity as measured by inter-press intervals.
claims.source: Importantly prolonged inhibition did not result in decreased motor activity; Figure (7B top) shows histograms of the inter-press intervals (IPIs) for the two conditions in which there appears to be no discernable difference. A two sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the cumulative distributions of the IPIs (Figure 7B bottom) revealed no significant effect (D(1436,1045) = 0.028, p=0.74).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 7B.

claims.claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed no effect of inactivation on food consumption.
claims.source: To do this, animals were given a bowl of 20 grams of food pellets in the conditioning box for 30 min to assess pellet consumption with and without inhibition. This test was repeated 4 times with blocked and patent cables (counterbalanced). A repeated measures ANOVA (with rat and run as blocking factors) showed no effect of inactivation on food consumption (F(1,10) = 0.20, p=0.66).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claims.claim: Transient optogenetic inactivation of medial OFC on randomly selected trials had no effect on economic choice behavior.
claims.source: In the current study, we employed a rodent version of the economic choice task used to demonstrate neural correlates of economic value in primates (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006) to test whether medial OFC makes a critical contribution to economic choice behavior. We found that transient optogenetic inactivation of medial OFC on randomly selected trials had no effect.
claims.evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by all the statistical analyses presented.

claims.claim: Inactivation in the same rats altered performance on a progressive ratio task known to be sensitive to medial OFC manipulations.
claims.source: Inactivation in the same rats altered performance on a progressive ratio task known to be sensitive to medial OFC manipulations, and post-mortem testing confirmed that medial OFC neurons in these rats exhibited viral expression and light-sensitive reduction in spiking activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the progressive ratio data and the electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: Post-mortem testing confirmed that medial OFC neurons in these rats exhibited viral expression and light-sensitive reduction in spiking activity.
claims.source: Inactivation in the same rats altered performance on a progressive ratio task known to be sensitive to medial OFC manipulations, and post-mortem testing confirmed that medial OFC neurons in these rats exhibited viral expression and light-sensitive reduction in spiking activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the histology and electrophysiology data.

claims.claim: Medial OFC is not necessary for economic choice in well-trained rats.
claims.source: Together these data show that the medial OFC is not necessary for economic choice in well-trained rats.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the combined results.

claims.claim: The current study builds on a prior report that optogenetic inactivation of lateral OFC also had no discernable effect on economic choice.
claims.source: The current study builds on our prior report that optogenetic inactivation of lateral OFC also had no discernable effect on economic choice in this setting (Gardner et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior published work.

claims.claim: Inactivation of lateral OFC was motivated by reports that neural activity in lateral OFC correlates with value during economic choice.
claims.source: Inactivation of lateral OFC was motivated by influential reports that neural activity in lateral OFC correlates with value during economic choice (McGinty et al., 2016; Padoa-Schioppa, 2009; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2008; Rich and Wallis, 2016; Tremblay and Schultz, 1999; Xie and Padoa-Schioppa, 2016), and the associated proposal that lateral OFC was central to normal decision-making in this context (Padoa-Schioppa, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claims.claim: Economic value is proposed to be equivalent to the value revealed by devaluation underlying model-based behavior.
claims.source: Implicit in this proposal is that economic value is equivalent to the value revealed by devaluation underlying so-called model-based behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an implicit assumption identified by the authors in the neuroeconomics framework.

claims.claim: Model-based behavior typically depends on lateral OFC in both rats and primates.
claims.source: Such behavior typically depends on this part of OFC in both rats and primates (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Machado and Bachevalier, 2007; Pickens et al., 2005; Pickens et al., 2003; Rudebeck et al., 2013; West et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in rats and primates.

claims.claim: Lateral OFC inactivation abolished changes in behavior due to devaluation without any effect on economic choice behavior.
claims.source: Yet we found that we could inactivate lateral OFC and abolish changes in behavior due to devaluation without any effect on economic choice behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the authors' prior experimental results.

claims.claim: The result that lateral OFC inactivation did not affect economic choice did not support lateral OFC as a critical, single bottleneck for calculating economic value.
claims.source: While this result did not support the lateral OFC as a critical, single bottleneck in which economic value is calculated, it left open whether other parts of the OFC might be performing this function.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the prior experimental results.

claims.claim: The OFC is now recognized to be a large area, potentially divisible into discrete subregions mediating discrete functions.
claims.source: The OFC is now recognized to be a large area, potentially divisible into discrete subregions mediating discrete functions (Heilbronner et al., 2016; Izquierdo, 2017; Murphy and Deutch, 2018; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011b; Walton et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature on OFC organization.

claims.claim: Within the OFC framework, medial OFC is increasingly associated with representing value.
claims.source: Within this framework, the medial OFC is increasingly associated with representing value.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current understanding in the field.

claims.claim: Lesions to medial OFC in monkeys disrupt value-guided decisions whereas lateral OFC lesions cause deficits in other more subtle functions.
claims.source: Further, lesions to medial OFC in monkeys disrupt value-guided decisions whereas lateral OFC lesions on the same behavior cause deficits in other more subtle functions, such as credit-assignment (Noonan et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in monkeys.

claims.claim: Medial OFC is necessary for appropriate valuation during acquisition of cue-outcome pairings.
claims.source: Other studies have shown that medial OFC is necessary for appropriate valuation during acquisition of cue-outcome pairings (Baylis and Gaffan, 1991), and also following selective satiation of one outcome during a choice task (Rudebeck and Murray, 2011a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on medial OFC function.

claims.claim: Damage to medial OFC in humans is associated with deficits in valuation and changes in economic decision-making.
claims.source: Damage to medial OFC in humans is associated with similar deficits, as well as changes in economic decision-making (Camille et al., 2011; Fellows and Farah, 2007; Noonan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human lesion studies.

claims.claim: Despite promising background data, inactivating medial OFC had no effect on economic choice.
claims.source: Yet despite the promising background data, we again failed to find any effect of inactivating the OFC on economic choice.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claims.claim: Rats exhibited similar preferences among groups of flavored food pellets with or without medial OFC online.
claims.source: Rats exhibited similar preferences among groups of flavored food pellets with or without medial OFC online, at least as indexed by indifference points, the steepness of the curves relating the two pellets, and the transitivity of the choices.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results across multiple measures.

claims.claim: There was a reduction in the progressive ratio breakpoint with medial OFC inactivation.
claims.source: This was true despite a reduction in the progressive ratio breakpoint in the same rats with inactivation, an effect that would traditionally be interpreted as an effect on valuation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the progressive ratio data.

claims.claim: The results show that medial OFC is not the critical bottleneck for calculating a single common currency value to guide economic choice.
claims.source: These results show that medial OFC is also not the critical bottleneck for calculating a single common currency value to guide economic choice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results.

claims.claim: The data point strongly to the possibility that economic value and resultant decision-making depend on parallel processing in multiple regions.
claims.source: Instead, these and the prior data point strongly to the possibility that economic value and the resultant decision-making depend on parallel processing in multiple regions (Hunt and Hayden, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, supported by citation to a relevant theoretical paper.

claims.claim: Parallel processing would be predicted if the value judgement underlying economic choice reflected a variety of associative information.
claims.source: Such parallel processing would be predicted if the value judgement underlying economic choice, at least as assayed in this task, reflected a variety of associative information (e.g. Pavlovian and instrumental, model-based and model-free, habitual and goal-directed).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the results.

claims.claim: The economic choice task used here does not try to limit or control the associative information at play.
claims.source: This is likely because the economic choice task used here, and those employed in other settings, generally do not try to limit or control the associative information at play.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the task design.

claims.claim: Different types of associative information do not generally converge into a single common brain region but are mediated by somewhat non-overlapping brain circuits.
claims.source: Tasks that employ such controls have clearly demonstrated that these different types of associative information do not generally converge into a single common brain region, but instead are mediated by somewhat non-overlapping brain circuits, each capable of mediating behavior somewhat independently, particularly in simple or poorly-controlled settings.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The results are more consistent with a distributed representation of value.
claims.source: Our results are more consistent with this sort of distributed representation of value.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of existing theories.

claims.claim: The processing in lateral and medial OFC may still be important for economic choice behavior, but a better controlled task is necessary to reveal the critical contributions.
claims.source: Of course, this does not mean that the processing demonstrated in this and similar tasks in lateral and medial OFC is not important for economic choice behavior. Rather it simply means that a better controlled form of the task is necessary in order to reveal the critical contributions these areas (and others) each make to the very general function of economic choice.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about future research directions.

claims.claim: It has been suggested that orbital areas are critical when choices are novel, rapidly changing, or involve elements that have never been experienced.
claims.source: For example, it has been suggested that orbital areas are critical when choices are novel, rapidly changing, or involve elements that have never been experienced – such as the evocative tea-jelly and snail-porridge prepared by Behrens and colleagues (Baylis and Gaffan, 1991; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011b; Fellows and Farah, 2007; Noonan et al., 2010); Chau et al., 2014; Barron et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies suggesting this role for orbital areas.

claims.claim: The dissociation between economic choice and OFC-dependent behaviors occurs because these behaviors require a form of inference or estimation not necessary in a well-trained subject in the standard economic choice task.
claims.source: Viewed in this light, the dissociation here (and also in our prior study) between economic choice and OFC-dependent behaviors, such as progressive ratio and Pavlovian devaluation for lOFC, occurs because these behaviors require a form of inference or estimation that is not necessary in a well-trained subject in the standard economic choice task like that used here.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the dissociation observed in the results.

claims.claim: Economic choices will depend on a particular region to the extent the choice emphasizes the processing dependent on that area.
claims.source: Economic choices will depend on a particular region to the extent the choice emphasizes the processing dependent on that area.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical statement about how brain regions contribute to economic choice.

claims.claim: The role of different subregions within OFC in economic choice behavior would be identical to their roles in other value-based behaviors.
claims.source: In this regard, the role of different subregions within OFC in economic choice behavior would be identical to their roles in other value-based behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical statement about OFC function.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior literature on the role of OFC in economic choice, noting that while neural correlates of value have been reported in OFC, these findings are inconsistent and causal evidence is sparse.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 accurately summarize the state of the field based on appropriate citations. The authors correctly identify both supporting evidence (C1-C2) and limitations (C3-C4) in prior work, providing balanced context for their study.

results.result: Prior work by the authors showed that optogenetic inactivation of lateral OFC did not affect economic choice in rats despite disrupting devaluation-sensitive Pavlovian responding.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 are supported by citations to the authors' prior published work (Gardner, 2017; Miller et al., 2018). This establishes the rationale for testing medial OFC and provides important context for interpreting the current results.

results.result: The manuscript reviews evidence that medial OFC, as a distinct subregion, is implicated in value signaling and value-guided behavior across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 are well-supported by multiple citations to relevant literature across human imaging, lesion studies, and animal models. This provides strong motivation for testing medial OFC specifically in the economic choice task.

results.result: Six male Long-Evans rats were trained on an economic choice task adapted from monkey studies, in which rats chose between different numbers of flavored food pellets presented as visual symbols on touchscreens.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C19 provide clear methodological details about subjects and task design, supported by direct descriptions and Figure 1A. The task design is appropriately adapted from established primate paradigms (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).

results.result: Rats displayed rational economic choice behavior characterized by stable indifference points ranging from 1:1 to >8:1, exhibiting transitivity across offer pairs, suggesting choices based on internal subjective values.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C27 describe baseline behavioral characteristics supported by prior publication (Gardner et al., 2017) and established economic theory (C27). The wide range of indifference points (C23) and demonstration of transitivity (C26) provide evidence for rational choice behavior.

results.result: AAV-CaMKIIa-eNpHR3.0-eYFP was bilaterally infused into medial OFC with fiberoptic probes implanted above injection sites. After recovery and retraining, rats underwent 8 weeks of testing with counterbalanced blocked/patent cables and laser-on/off trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C37 provide detailed methodological information about surgical procedures, viral vectors, optogenetic parameters, and experimental design. The use of blocked cables as controls (C32) and the 300ms ramp-down protocol (C37, supported by Chuong et al., 2014) demonstrate appropriate experimental rigor.

results.result: Medial OFC inactivation had no significant effect on indifference points. Two-way ANOVA revealed no main effects or interactions, with only a 0.3% change in IP during laser-on trials, well within confidence intervals.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 present the primary negative result with appropriate statistical analyses (n=50 sessions). The effect size is minimal (0.3%, C42), the test had adequate power to detect meaningful changes (C43), and results were consistent with eYFP controls (C40). Statistical reporting is complete and appropriate.

results.result: Excluding sessions with IPs close to 1:1 and analyzing data across time blocks or early in sessions still revealed no significant effects of medial OFC inactivation on indifference points.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 demonstrate robustness of the null result through multiple secondary analyses. The exclusion of near-equal preferences (C44), temporal analysis (C45-C46), and early-session analysis (C47) all support the primary finding. These analyses address potential confounds appropriately.

results.result: Medial OFC inactivation had no significant effect on inverse slope (choice variability). Two-way ANOVA revealed no main effects or interactions across multiple analyses, though a significant laser effect appeared in early-session blocked-fiber trials only.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C56 show that choice precision was unaffected by inactivation across full sessions and most analyses. The single significant effect (C56) occurred only in the control (blocked fiber) condition, suggesting it is not due to neural inactivation. Statistical analyses are comprehensive and appropriately reported.

results.result: Medial OFC inactivation did not affect transitivity of choices across pellet pairs. Rats maintained consistent value mappings with only small random fluctuations between laser-on and laser-off trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 demonstrate that value consistency across sessions was preserved during inactivation. Statistical analyses (C62-C63) show no effects on transitivity values or distances between paired points. This provides additional evidence that medial OFC is not necessary for maintaining stable value representations.

results.result: Ex vivo electrophysiology confirmed that 593 nm light significantly hyperpolarized medial OFC neurons expressing NpHR-YFP and reduced spike firing in response to current injection.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 provide critical positive control data demonstrating that the optogenetic manipulation was effective. Statistical analyses confirm significant hyperpolarization (C64, p=5.0e-4) and reduced firing (C66, p=0.01; C67, p=1.0e-4). This validates the inactivation approach and strengthens interpretation of behavioral null results.

results.result: Medial OFC inactivation significantly reduced progressive ratio breakpoint and total lever presses without affecting motor activity (inter-press intervals) or food consumption.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 provide essential positive control showing the same manipulation that failed to affect economic choice did impair progressive ratio performance (C68, p=0.01; C70, p=0.02), a task known to depend on medial OFC. The lack of motor (C71) or consumption (C72) effects rules out non-specific performance deficits.

results.result: Transient optogenetic inactivation of medial OFC had no effect on economic choice behavior in the same rats that showed impaired progressive ratio performance and confirmed viral expression with light-sensitive neural inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 synthesize the main findings. The dissociation between economic choice (unaffected) and progressive ratio (impaired) in the same animals with confirmed effective inactivation (C74-C75) provides strong evidence that medial OFC is not necessary for economic choice in well-trained rats (C76).

results.result: Combined with prior work showing lateral OFC inactivation also did not affect economic choice despite disrupting devaluation-sensitive behavior, these results challenge the view of OFC as a critical bottleneck for calculating economic value.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 appropriately contextualize current findings with prior work. The dissociation between economic choice and devaluation tasks (C81) across both lateral and medial OFC challenges the assumption that these processes reflect equivalent value computations (C79, C82).

results.result: Despite evidence that medial OFC represents value and is necessary for various value-guided behaviors, inactivation had no effect on economic choice (indifference points, slopes, transitivity) even though it reduced progressive ratio breakpoint.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C91 synthesize the paradox: medial OFC has strong associations with value processing (C83-C87) yet inactivation spared economic choice (C88-C89) while affecting progressive ratio (C90). This dissociation (C91) is the key finding challenging single-bottleneck models of value computation.

results.result: The results support a distributed, parallel processing model of economic value rather than a single common currency bottleneck, consistent with economic choice reflecting multiple types of associative information mediated by non-overlapping circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 present a theoretical interpretation of the null results. While the data are consistent with parallel processing (C92, C96), this remains one possible explanation among others. The claims about associative information (C93-C95) are reasonable but speculative, as the task was not designed to dissociate these processes (C94).

results.result: OFC processing may still be important for economic choice under specific conditions requiring inference or estimation (e.g., novel choices), and better-controlled tasks are needed to reveal the specific contributions of different OFC subregions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 offer speculative interpretations about when OFC might be necessary for economic choice. While these are reasonable hypotheses for future work (C97-C98), they remain untested. The proposal that well-trained subjects don't require OFC-dependent inference (C99) is plausible but not directly demonstrated.
